content.title: Back to the mistake
content.text: The network read this 7 as a 9. Nothing inside is broken: its 2,778 numbers were simply never nudged with this picture in mind. Look at the end of it only: the sixteen neurons of the last row, and the ten scores they feed.
content.ledger:
THE KNOB SO FAR
the 7, read as 9: 9 at 99.1%, 7 at 0.2%

content.title: One wire, one number
content.text: Pick one wire: from one of those sixteen neurons to the score for 7. On it sits one weight, 1.42, one of the 2,778 numbers. Nothing about it is special. It is just a number, and a number can be turned.
content.ledger:
THE KNOB SO FAR
the 7, read as 9: 9 at 99.1%, 7 at 0.2%
one wire · w = 1.42

content.title: Turn it
content.text: Turn it to the right and the 7’s score falls to nothing. Turn it to the left and the score climbs: 5.2% at −2, 25.3% at −4, 67.6% at −6, where the 7 finally wins. Left, not right, because the neuron on this wire holds a negative number, −0.91, and the wire multiplies: negative times negative is positive. Every weight has a direction that helps, and it is not always the obvious one.

content.title: A curve appears
content.text: Do it again and keep the record. For every value of the knob there is exactly one score. Lay the knob values left to right and the scores up and down, and the record is a curve. That curve is a function: a rule that takes one number in and gives one number out. Nothing more mysterious than that.

content.title: x in, y out
content.text: The names everyone uses. The number in is x, the number out is y, and the rule is f, so y = f(x). This point is the network as it stands: x = 1.42, y = 0.2%. Every x, y and f in the next pills means exactly this: one knob, one curve, one point on it.

content.title: Which way, and how far
content.text: From this point the curve rises to the left, so this knob should move left. But not far. At −1 the network gets 1,725 of the 1,797 test pictures right, one more than before. At −6 this 7 is fixed and 109 other pictures break: 1,615 right. A small move in the right direction helps everyone; a big one helps one picture and hurts the rest.

content.title: The question for every knob
content.text: Which way, and how far. For one knob the curve shows it at a glance. For 2,778 knobs nobody can draw 2,778 curves and look. There has to be a way to read the direction and the size of the step straight from the numbers. Building that reader is what the next pills do, one piece at a time, starting with the shapes these curves are made of.
